TESTIMONY BEFORE THE ENERGY, UTILITIES AND TECHNOLOGY COMMITTEE
Resolve, to Establish the Commission to Ensure a Just and Equitable Energy Transition to Maine's Workforce
L.D. 1420
GOVERNOR'S ENERGY OFFICE
April 16, 2025
Senator Lawrence, Representative Sachs, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Energy,
Utilities and Technology (EUT): My name is Caroline Colan, and I am the Legislative Liaison for the
Governor's Energy Office (GEO).
The GEO testifies neither for nor against L.D. 1420.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this proposal. LD. 1420 establishes a thirteenmember commission to "ensure a just and equitable energy transition for Maine's workforce." The Resolve directs the commission to meet six times to review and evaluate the state's current workforce; consider how to meet the expected demand for clean energy workers needed to meet the state's energy goals; consider salary and benefits associated with these jobs; to review efforts to support the transition of workers from one industry to another; to consider the economic impacts of the energy transition; to consider the benefits of a well-compensated workforce; and to examine how a statewide efforts to establish greater coordination on this topic may be beneficial to advancing the objectives of
the commission.
Should this bill be passed, it would likely become effective in late September or early October, at which point appointments to the commission must be made within 30 days. A final report to the EUT Committee must be submitted by February 1, 2026. Within these constraints, the commission will likely have November through January to conduct their review, develop recommendations, and deliver the final report to the Legislature. Given the limited number of meetings and timeframe to complete the work as outlined in this bill, the Committee should carefully consider what existing information the commission may seek to inform recommendations, what original information the group may wish to pursue, and whether conducting this work and advancing the objectives of the proposal through an existing forum could yield more fulsome results, avoid duplicative efforts, and provide adequate time to consider available and new information to make recommendations.
The appendix of this testimony contains a brief description of Maine's energy employment landscape today, a list of some pertinent existing research and forums where information on these topics can be gathered, and information about a few of the existing committees and structures in state government

Existing committees/structures that could support the objectives of the commission:
MDOL, GEO, the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF), the Maine Department of Education (DOE), the Maine Department of Transportation (DOT), and the Maine Department of Economic and Community Development (DECD) each contribute subject-matter expertise and conduct work on issues related to workforce policy, including some work that specifically focuses on infrastructure workforce.
GEO - Clean Energy Partnership: Maine's Clean Energy Partnership was established to advance
Maine's clean energy, climate, economic development, and workforce goals -- including the
Governor's goal of doubling Maine's clean energy and energy efficiency jobs by 2030. GEO has
created an Advisory Group to work with leading experts to sustain attention and promote collaboration to address emerging needs, build new and expand existing supply chains, and support opportunities for Maine in these fast-growing fields.
o Since 2022, GEO has awarded federal grant funds through the Clean Energy Partnership for
clean energy workforce development and training programs. Programs have been launched across the state to support and prepare thousands of Maine people for careers in the state's rapidly growing clean energy sector, attracting new workers to the clean energy and energy efficiency workforce, providing career training and upskilling, and facilitating entry into the clean energy job market.
Governor's Workforce Cabinet: The Governor's Workforce Cabinet convenes representatives from the MDOL, DECD, DOE, DHHS, GOPIF, and the University of Maine and Maine Community College System on workforce~related topics to foster collaboration and ensure alignment of efforts. The
priority areas of focus of the Cabinet include growing local talent with a focus on the New Mainer community, attracting new talent with a focus on defining specific populations and aligning policy
and programs to support those communities, and aligning systems to inform a coordinated response
to budgetary, funding & policy shifts, or new opportunities.
MDOL Infrastructure Workforce Alignment -- Working Group: An inter-agency working group that
seeks to collaborate around investing in and strengthening our infrastructure workforce to 1) advance our climate resiliency, clean energy, and economic development goals and 2) take advantage of federal funding by staying in touch on potential funding opportunities with an infrastructure workforce lens, aligning on shared workforce priorities, and identifying opportunities to leverage and strengthen ongoing workforce development efforts.
The Maine Climate Council and the Equity Subcommittee: In June 2019, Governorlanet Mills signed LD 1679 into law, with strong bipartisan support from the Maine Legislature, to establish increased

Edgelynn Venuti Orono, ME Monday, April 14th, 2025 To the Board of Trustees, Office of the President, and UMaine Campus Community,
From: Edgelynn Venuti Re: UMaine Orono Waste & Recycling Practices
I am a second year student here at UMaine studying Ecology and Environmental Sciences. I was disheartened to hear about the proposed transition to a single-stream recycling system. I have been under the impression that UMaine no longer had a recycling system in place and that any attempts to sort on campus were wasted as it was combined with trash later in the process. I know I am not the only student who believes this, indicating a strong need for enhanced education around recycling initiatives on campus.
However, increased education is not all that is needed. UMaine also needs to continue its commitment to having a recycling program in place that actually recycles. Switching to the proposed single-stream recycling system would not fulfill this need. The board should consider the long-term impacts of this decision. The climate crisis is already a pressing issue and we need to focus on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, not creating more. With UMaine choosing to divest from fossil fuels only a few years ago now, this choice backtracks on those moral efforts. Consider the longevity of the natural health and well-being of this beautiful state we call home.
Please at the very least consider utilizing current recycling efforts and make an effort to expand on-campus education about recycling efforts. If capacity is an issue, connect with student organizations such as Waste Minimizers. There are so many passionate people here willing to step up to ensure that UMaine is a clean, sustainable campus. Another consideration is for UMaine to transition to the Hampden separate trash and recycling stem which is more cost-effective than the existing program and only 4,000 dollars more than the single-stream program under consideration.
I urge you to continue and make efforts to expand upon UMaine's recycling program and education and reject the proposal to switch to a single-stream recycling system.
Respectfully submitted, Edgelynn Venuti

Chairs Lawrence, Sachs and members of the Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology, my name is Jason J. Shedlock, l live in Portland and l'm pleased to offer my testimony in support of LD 1420. l'd like to extend special
thanks to Senator Lawrence for his leadership in introducing this bill, as well as Representatives Geiger and Kessler, along with Senator Tipping for co-sponsoring it.
I stand before you in my role as President of the Maine Building Trades, Regional Organizer & Secretary-Treasurer
of Local 327 of the Laborers' Union, President of the Southern Maine Labor Council, among other roles and responsibilities, all of which afford me the honor of representing tens of thousands of working Mainers.
lt is those working Mainers -- and the ones that will come after them - that I have in mind when l let you know how
critically important it is for this state to have a comprehensive, collaborative and cogent energy transition policy
that actually takes into account the human beings that we will need to meet the administration's mounting
number of goals for Maine's energy future.
This committee understood this when, just over a year ago, you voted to pass LD 2077; a bill that included a very
similar framework to what you have before you today. We know that in one form or another, the historically solid
middle-class careers - with fair pay and good benefits like healthcare and retirement - of Maine's carbon-based energy economy will continue to give way to the move towards electrification, and the unpredictable swings in labor standards and compensation that we've seen come with it.
We cannot be serious about reaching our energy goals if we don't get serious about the way we treat the Mainers who will be expected to help us meet them. We cannot lament an alleged workforce shortage while at the same
time only pay attention to job quality and working conditions when we are forced to do so by the people who
write the checks that fund the projects.
But you knew this last year, and you acted decisively. Then, it was labor, along with our allies in the environmental movement and the energy industry, that formulated a solution that has largely informed what's before you today. l am encouraged by the priority that has been placed on a just and equitable energy transition by many in the legislature this session - including the thoughtful efforts made by members of this committee. l would be pleased to work with the committee between now and the work session to ensure this bill is best informed by those
efforts and ideas.
We're told that "Maine Won't Wait." So naturally l would have hoped that the language before you, or a version of
it, would have been prioritized as a part of the administration's legislative agenda for this session (especially as we stand up a new Department to expand our efforts). It wasn't. So yet again we turn to this Committee to offer a
pathway forward.
l urge the Committee to pass LD 1420.

Testimony of Senator Mark W. Lawrence introducing
LD 1420, Resolve, to Establish the Commission to Ensure a Just and Equitable Energy
Transition for Maine's Workforce
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities and Technology
April 16, 2025
Chair Sachs and esteemed colleagues of the Joint Standing Committee on Energy, Utilities and
Technology, my name is Mark Lawrence. I am the State Senator from District 35 in southern York County, proudly representing Eliot, Kittery, Ogunquit, South Berwick, and York. I am here today to present LD 1420, Resolve, to Establish the Commission to Ensure a Just and Equitable
Energy Transition for Maine's Workforce.
As Maine transitions from our heavy reliance on fossil fuels towards a clean energy future in an effort to preserve our planet and lower future costs, we must do so with integrity and
consideration for the hardworking men and women who will help us get there. We must ensure
that the workers of today and tomorrow have quality training and safe working conditions to complete these projects. That is the goal of the bill before you today.
LD 1420 would establish and convene the Commission to Ensure a Just and Equitable Energy
Transition for Maine's Workforce. The Commission will evaluate Maine's current energy workforce, including compensation and benefits, and assess workforce demands to meet the State's energy goals. It will also examine the types and numbers of jobs needed, analyze current pay and benefits for those roles, and review efforts to ensure a just and equitable transition for energy workers--such as minimizing compensation loss, identifying transferable skills, and
addressing training needs.
Additionally, the Commission will consider the economic impact of the energy transition on low-
income ratepayers and explore how a well-compensated workforce supports state energy
obj ectives. Lastly, it will evaluate the potential benefits of establishing a coordinated statewide entity or framework to guide a just transition for workers and support employers in the energy
sector.
The Commission would include bipartisan representation from the Maine Senate and House, members of the public working in labor, energy and environmental fields, the Maine Apprenticeship Council, the Governor's Office and the Public Utilities Commission.
